Shares are sold gradually into the open market through a sales agent
Pricing is set by Dutch auction among retail bidders

explanation: ABBs quickly gather institutional demand and set final price/volume in days or hours. The short window reduces market risk.

distractorExplanations.b: A two-week roadshow is a fully marketed offering; an ABB is launched and priced within hours.
distractorExplanations.c: Gradual sales through an agent describe an at-the-market program, not an accelerated bookbuild.
distractorExplanations.d: ABBs are priced by underwriters from institutional demand, not via a retail Dutch auction.

prompt: A 144A-for-life high-yield bond is sold:

options.text: To accredited investors under Rule 506(c)
To qualified institutional buyers under Rule 144A
To retail investors after an A/B exchange offer
To non-U.S. investors under Regulation S only

explanation: 144A-for-life relies on QIB private placement exemptions for both issuance and trading restrictions. No subsequent SEC registration for resale follows.

distractorExplanations.a: Rule 506(c) is a Reg D issuer exemption with verification; 144A-for-life bonds are resold to QIBs.
distractorExplanations.c: An A/B exchange offer registers the bonds; 144A-for-life deals skip that registration step.
distractorExplanations.d: Many 144A deals have a Reg S tranche, but the 144A-for-life label refers to the QIB resale market.

prompt: An at-the-market (ATM) equity program lets an issuer:

options.text: Sell a large block overnight at a discount to institutions
Offer new shares to existing holders at a fixed discount
Sell shares into the open market at prevailing prices
Buy back shares in the open market under Rule 10b-18

explanation: ATMs dribble out primary shares opportunistically with lower market impact than block deals. Sales run through a sales agent over time.

distractorExplanations.a: An overnight discounted block is an accelerated bookbuild, not a dribble-out ATM program.
distractorExplanations.b: Offering new shares pro rata to existing holders at a discount is a rights offering.
distractorExplanations.d: Rule 10b-18 repurchases buy shares back; an ATM sells new primary shares.

prompt: In a best-efforts underwriting, the underwriter:

options.text: Buys the full issue and resells it to the public
Buys only the shares left after a rights offering
Guarantees a minimum price for 30 days after listing
Uses commercially reasonable efforts to sell securities

explanation: Best efforts shift unsold risk to the issuer; firm commitment underwriters buy the offering. The underwriter does not commit to buy unsold shares.

distractorExplanations.a: Buying the full issue and reselling it is a firm commitment, not a best-efforts underwriting.
distractorExplanations.b: Buying shares left after a rights offering is a standby commitment, not best efforts.
distractorExplanations.c: No underwriting form guarantees aftermarket prices; stabilization is limited by Regulation M.

prompt: IPO lock-up agreements typically restrict:

options.text: Company insiders and major shareholders from selling shares
Underwriter analysts from publishing research on the issuer
The issuer from paying dividends until profitable
New investors from flipping IPO shares in the first week

explanation: Lock-ups reduce post-IPO supply pressure from pre-IPO holders and align with stabilization period. The restriction runs for a period after the offering.

distractorExplanations.b: Research quiet periods arise under FINRA Rule 2241, not from insider lock-up agreements.
distractorExplanations.c: Dividend restrictions come from credit agreements, not from IPO lock-up agreements.
distractorExplanations.d: Lock-ups bind pre-IPO holders; flipping by IPO buyers is discouraged by penalty bids, not lock-ups.

prompt: A dual-tranche bond offering might include:

options.text: Common stock alongside warrants in a units offering
Senior secured notes alongside senior unsecured notes
A term loan B alongside a revolving credit facility
Convertible notes alongside a stock repurchase

explanation: Issuers split credit risk tiers to broaden investor demand and optimize pricing. Tranches differ in collateral packages and yields.

distractorExplanations.a: Stock with warrants is an equity units offering, not two tranches of bonds.
distractorExplanations.c: Term loans and revolvers are bank loan facilities, not bond tranches in a note offering.
distractorExplanations.d: A convertible paired with a buyback is an equity-linked trade, not a dual-tranche bond deal.

prompt: Green bond issuers commit to allocate proceeds toward:

options.text: Eligible social projects such as affordable housing and community health care
General corporate purposes as long as the issuer has a climate target
Eligible environmental projects tracked and often reported to investors
Any project once the bond is rated investment grade

explanation: Green-labeled bonds tie use of proceeds to climate or environmental projects per framework (e.g., ICMA principles).

distractorExplanations.a: Proceeds for social projects define social bonds; green bonds fund environmental projects.
distractorExplanations.b: Bonds tied to company-wide climate targets are sustainability-linked; green bonds ring-fence proceeds.
distractorExplanations.d: Credit rating has nothing to do with use of proceeds; green bonds fund eligible environmental projects.

prompt: Rule 10b5-1 trading plans allow insiders to:

options.text: Modify scheduled plan trades at will after learning material nonpublic information
Start trading the day after adoption with no cooling-off period
Avoid filing Form 4 for transactions executed under the plan
Pre-schedule trades under a written plan adopted when not in possession of MNPI

explanation: Affirmative defense plans set automatic sales/purchases to reduce appearance of trading on MNPI. The plan must be adopted in good faith.

distractorExplanations.a: Modifying a plan while holding MNPI destroys the affirmative defense and counts as a new adoption.
distractorExplanations.b: Since the 2022 amendments, officers and directors face a cooling-off period of at least 90 days before trading.
distractorExplanations.c: Plan trades by Section 16 insiders still require Form 4 reporting within two business days.

prompt: An incurrence covenant in bond indentures typically allows additional debt only if:

options.text: Pro forma financial tests (e.g., leverage or coverage ratios) are satisfied
The ratio test is met at every quarter-end, whether or not new debt is added
Bondholders holding a majority consent to each new borrowing
The issuer's credit rating stays at investment grade

explanation: Incurrence tests gate new debt on credit metrics; maintenance covenants require ongoing compliance.

distractorExplanations.b: Testing every quarter-end without any triggering action is a maintenance covenant; incurrence tests apply when debt is incurred.
distractorExplanations.c: Consent solicitations amend indentures; incurrence covenants permit debt that meets ratio tests without a vote.
distractorExplanations.d: Rating-based fall-away provisions are different; incurrence covenants turn on pro forma ratios.

prompt: An equity carve-out IPO involves:

options.text: Distributing all of the subsidiary's shares to the parent's holders tax-free
Selling a minority stake in a subsidiary while the parent retains control
Selling the subsidiary outright to a private equity buyer
Listing the parent's shares on a second foreign exchange

explanation: Carve-outs monetize a division and establish public currency while parent keeps majority ownership.

distractorExplanations.a: Distributing subsidiary shares to existing holders is a spin-off, not an IPO carve-out.
distractorExplanations.c: An outright sale to a sponsor is a divestiture; a carve-out sells a minority stake via IPO.
distractorExplanations.d: A dual listing of parent shares raises no subsidiary equity; it is not a carve-out.

prompt: Fintech issuer Northloop plans a $25 million raise, to be advertised on LinkedIn and its website, and will sell to accredited investors exclusively. Which offering exemption fits?

options.text: Rule 506(b), since every buyer will be accredited
Rule 506(c), verifying each buyer's accredited status
Regulation Crowdfunding, as it permits online advertising
Rule 504, which lets issuers advertise in any state

explanation: The general-solicitation track of Rule 506 permits public online ads if every purchaser is accredited and the issuer takes reasonable steps to verify that status, not just a self-certification. Rule 506 has no dollar cap, so a $25 million raise fits.

distractorExplanations.a: The traditional Rule 506 track bars general solicitation even when all buyers are accredited, so public LinkedIn and website ads would break it.
distractorExplanations.c: Regulation Crowdfunding caps raises at $5 million in 12 months and must run through a registered portal, far below $25 million.
distractorExplanations.d: Rule 504 caps offerings at $10 million in 12 months and allows general solicitation only under qualifying state registration.

prompt: Liability management exercises (e.g., debt tender offers) often aim to:

options.text: Issue new senior bonds to fund an acquisition of a competitor
Convert all outstanding bonds to equity by court order in Chapter 11
Increase leverage to fund a special dividend
Refinance or extend maturities, reduce coupons, or amend covenants

explanation: LM transactions restructure outstanding bonds when issuers seek lower cost or flexibility. These changes are made with holder consent.

distractorExplanations.a: Issuing bonds to fund an acquisition is new-money financing, not liability management of existing debt.
distractorExplanations.b: Court-ordered conversion is a Chapter 11 plan outcome; LM exercises are consensual and out of court.
distractorExplanations.c: Borrowing for a special dividend is a dividend recap, not a liability management transaction.

prompt: Stapled financing offered by a sell-side advisor provides:

options.text: Pre-arranged debt commitment letters bidders can use to fund the acquisition
Seller financing in which the target's owners carry a note
An equity backstop from the sell-side bank's private equity arm
A bridge loan the target itself draws to refinance its debt before the sale closes

explanation: Stapled packages speed auction certainty but may create conflicts managed through disclosure and Chinese walls.

distractorExplanations.b: A seller note is deferred consideration from the sellers, not a bank financing package stapled to the auction.
distractorExplanations.c: Stapled financing is debt offered to bidders, not an equity backstop from the bank.
distractorExplanations.d: Staple packages fund the buyer's acquisition, not the target's own refinancing before closing.

prompt: Reverse inquiry in a bond new-issue process refers to:

options.text: An issuer surveying investors with test-the-waters calls
An investor initiating interest in a potential offering
Underwriters gathering orders after the deal is launched
A rating agency querying the issuer during the roadshow

explanation: Reverse inquiry helps bankers gauge demand and structure for opportunistic or window offerings. The inquiry comes before the issuer formally launches.

distractorExplanations.a: Test-the-waters outreach is issuer-initiated; reverse inquiry starts with the investor.
distractorExplanations.c: Collecting orders after launch is bookbuilding, not investor-initiated reverse inquiry.
distractorExplanations.d: Rating agency questions are part of the rating process, not investor-driven demand.

prompt: In a follow-on, the company sells newly issued shares and existing holders sell some of their shares. Which statement is right?

options.text: Primary shares are newly issued and the cash goes to the company
Primary shares are sold by existing holders and the cash goes to those holders
Secondary shares are newly issued and the cash from them goes to the company
Existing holders sell the primary shares, and the company issues the secondary shares

explanation: Primary shares are newly issued by the company, so the cash proceeds go to the company and shares outstanding increase. Secondary shares are existing shares sold by current holders, so those holders receive the cash and the company does not issue new stock.

distractorExplanations.b: This assigns the holders' sale to primary. Shares sold by existing holders are secondary shares, and those holders, not the company, receive that cash.
distractorExplanations.c: This mislabels the new issue. Newly issued shares whose cash goes to the company are primary shares, not secondary shares.
distractorExplanations.d: This reverses the two categories. Existing holders sell secondary shares; the company sells primary shares and receives that cash.

prompt: A company launches an IPO with a base deal of 20 million shares. The overallotment option is limited to:

options.text: 2 million shares, equal to 10 percent of the base deal
3 million shares, equal to 15 percent of the base deal
4 million shares, equal to 20 percent of the base deal
5 million shares, equal to 25 percent of the base deal and set from the first-day close

explanation: The overallotment option is capped at 15 percent of the base deal, not a larger slice of it. Twenty million base shares times 15 percent is 3 million shares. The cap is a fraction of that base size.

distractorExplanations.a: Ten percent of the base is too small. The overallotment option is capped at 15 percent of the base deal, which is 3 million shares here.
distractorExplanations.c: Twenty percent overstates the option. The overallotment is limited to 15 percent of the base deal, or 3 million shares on this IPO.
distractorExplanations.d: Twenty-five percent is above the cap, and the option is not sized off the first-day close. The cap is 15 percent of the base deal.

prompt: The book is built and a marketed IPO is ready to price. What does the firm-commitment underwriter do?

options.text: Acts as agent and returns any unsold shares to the issuer
Buys the entire issue from the company before marketing begins, with no roadshow
Buys the shares at pricing and resells them, taking the price risk
Buys the shares left unsold when a rights offering expires

explanation: In a firm-commitment deal the underwriter buys the shares from the issuer at pricing and resells them to investors. The bank, not the company, takes the price risk if those shares cannot be resold at the offer price.

distractorExplanations.a: Returning unsold shares is best efforts, where the bank is an agent. A firm-commitment underwriter buys the shares at pricing and keeps the price risk.
distractorExplanations.b: Buying the whole issue before marketing is a bought deal. On a marketed IPO the firm-commitment purchase happens at pricing, after the book is built.
distractorExplanations.d: Buying the leftover shares after a rights offering is standby underwriting. A firm-commitment IPO is purchased at pricing and then resold.

prompt: Shares fall below the IPO price in the first trading sessions. What is aftermarket stabilization under Regulation M?

options.text: A promise that the stock will stay at or above the offer price
Open-market purchases made at prices above the public offering price
A 180-day resale ban that keeps IPO buyers from selling their allocated shares
A limited permitted bid, not a promise that the offer price will hold

explanation: Aftermarket stabilization under Regulation M is a limited permitted bid used to support trading after pricing. It is not a promise that the stock will stay at the offer price, and the shares can still fall through that price.

distractorExplanations.a: Stabilization is not a promise to hold the offer price. Regulation M allows a limited bid, and the stock can still trade below the offer price.
distractorExplanations.b: Stabilization is not a purchase campaign above the offer price. It is a limited permitted bid, and it does not guarantee the aftermarket price.
distractorExplanations.c: A 180-day hold on buyers confuses stabilization with a lock-up. Stabilization is a limited permitted bid, not a ban on resales by IPO buyers.

prompt: A company sets aside part of its registered IPO for customers. That directed share program is:

options.text: A reserved allocation of IPO shares for a named group such as customers
A separate registration exemption for the customers who buy those shares
A Regulation D private placement that runs beside the registered IPO
A pro rata rights offering made to the people who already hold the stock

explanation: A directed share program reserves a portion of the registered IPO for a named group, such as customers or friends and family. Those shares are still part of the registered offering. The program is not, by itself, a separate exemption from registration.

distractorExplanations.b: Reserving shares for customers does not create an exemption. Those shares are still sold under the IPO registration statement.
distractorExplanations.c: A directed share program is an allocation inside the registered IPO. It is not a separate Regulation D private placement.
distractorExplanations.d: A rights offering gives existing holders a pro rata purchase right. A directed share program reserves IPO shares for a named group such as customers.

prompt: A CEO publishes a post offering shares to the public before the registration statement is filed. That post is:

options.text: A permitted test-the-waters communication addressed to any public reader
Gun-jumping, an illegal offer before the registration rules allow it
A free writing prospectus, which the company may use before it files
Routine roadshow marketing that may begin as soon as the bookrunners are hired

explanation: Gun-jumping is an illegal offer to sell a security before the registration rules allow that offer. A public invitation to buy IPO shares, made before the registration statement is filed, is that kind of illegal offer.

distractorExplanations.a: Test-the-waters conversations are limited to institutional investors. A public post offering shares to retail readers before filing is gun-jumping.
distractorExplanations.c: A free writing prospectus is a written offer used after the registration statement is filed. It does not authorize this public offer before filing.
distractorExplanations.d: Hiring the banks does not open an offer window. A public offer to buy shares before the registration statement is filed is gun-jumping.

prompt: A U.S. company is registering its first sale of common stock to the public. Which registration form fits?

options.text: Form S-3, because a first-time issuer puts its IPO on the shelf
Form S-4, because the IPO is registered as an exchange offer to the public
Form S-1; Form S-3 is for a seasoned issuer's later offerings
Form S-8, because the IPO shares are treated as employee benefit-plan stock

explanation: A first-time issuer registers its IPO on Form S-1. Form S-3 is the short form for a seasoned issuer's later offerings, including many follow-on sales. A company selling stock to the public for the first time does not use Form S-3 for that IPO.

distractorExplanations.a: Form S-3 is for a seasoned issuer's later offerings. A first-time IPO is registered on Form S-1, and a new issuer does not put that IPO on an S-3 shelf.
distractorExplanations.b: Form S-4 registers mergers and exchange offers. The first sale of a company's shares to the public is an IPO on Form S-1.
distractorExplanations.d: Form S-8 registers shares issued under employee benefit plans. It is not the registration form for the company's IPO.

prompt: Bookrunners were hired months ago and the registration statement is on file. When is the underwriting agreement signed?

options.text: Signed at pricing, not when the issuer first picks the banks
When the issuer awards the mandate and names the bookrunners
When the registration statement is filed with the SEC for review
On the listing day, once the shares have printed their opening trade

explanation: The underwriting agreement is signed at pricing, when the price and size are set and the banks commit to buy the shares from the issuer. Selecting the bookrunners earlier is only a mandate, not that purchase commitment.

distractorExplanations.b: The mandate only chooses the banks. The underwriting agreement, which commits them to buy the shares, is signed at pricing.
distractorExplanations.c: Filing starts SEC review. It is not the moment the banks commit to purchase. That commitment is the underwriting agreement signed at pricing.
distractorExplanations.d: By the first trade the shares have already been sold under the agreement. The underwriting agreement is signed at pricing, before listing.

prompt: An IPO pays a gross spread of $1.00 per share. How is that spread typically divided?

options.text: $0.60 management fee, $0.20 underwriting fee, and $0.20 selling concession
$0.20 management fee, $0.60 underwriting fee, and $0.20 selling concession
$0.20 management fee, $0.20 underwriting fee, and $0.60 selling concession
$0.33 management fee, $0.33 underwriting fee, and $0.34 selling concession, divided in equal thirds

explanation: A typical IPO gross spread is divided about 20 percent management fee, 20 percent underwriting fee, and 60 percent selling concession. On a $1.00 spread those amounts are $0.20, $0.20, and $0.60. The selling concession is the largest piece.

distractorExplanations.a: This makes the management fee the largest piece. The usual split is 20 percent management fee, 20 percent underwriting fee, and 60 percent selling concession.
distractorExplanations.b: This makes the underwriting fee the largest piece. On a $1 spread the selling concession is the $0.60 piece, and the other two fees are $0.20 each.
distractorExplanations.d: An even split is not the convention. The selling concession is about 60 percent of the spread, $0.60 of this $1, and it is the largest piece.

prompt: Roadshow investors receive a prospectus that leaves the final price blank. That red herring is:

options.text: The final prospectus, already filled in with the price and the number of shares
The underwriting agreement, handed out on the roadshow in place of a prospectus
A free writing prospectus that the company may circulate before it files
The preliminary prospectus used on the roadshow, not the final prospectus

explanation: The red herring is the preliminary prospectus used to market the deal on the roadshow. It describes the offering but leaves the final price open. It is not the final prospectus, which includes the price and is used after pricing.

distractorExplanations.a: The final prospectus states the price and the size and is used after pricing. The red herring is the preliminary prospectus used on the roadshow.
distractorExplanations.b: The underwriting agreement is the contract signed at pricing. The red herring is the preliminary prospectus, not that contract.
distractorExplanations.c: A free writing prospectus is a separate written offer. The red herring is the preliminary prospectus itself, used on the roadshow after filing.

prompt: After the registration statement is filed, the desk emails a written term sheet offering the new bonds. That term sheet is:

options.text: An unrestricted written offer, proper even if it had been sent before filing
A substitute for the statutory prospectus, so buyers need no prospectus
A free writing prospectus, a written offer used after the statement is filed
The final prospectus, which the syndicate sends after the bonds have been priced

explanation: A free writing prospectus is a written offer, such as a term sheet, used after the registration statement has been filed. It is not an unrestricted offer the issuer may make before filing, and it does not replace the statutory prospectus.

distractorExplanations.a: A written offer before filing is not a free writing prospectus. The free writing prospectus is used after the registration statement has been filed.
distractorExplanations.b: A free writing prospectus does not replace the statutory prospectus. It is an additional written offer used after the registration statement is filed.
distractorExplanations.d: The final prospectus is the priced statutory prospectus. A term sheet emailed as a written offer after filing is a free writing prospectus, not that final document.

prompt: The syndicate oversold the IPO by the overallotment amount, and the stock then trades below the offer price. How do they cover the short?

options.text: They buy shares in the market, below the offer price, to cover the short
They exercise the option and buy the extra shares from the issuer at the offer price
They have the issuer cancel the overallotment and refund the buyers of the IPO
They sell more shares into the falling market and leave a larger short position

explanation: If the stock trades down, the underwriters cover the greenshoe short by buying shares in the market. If the stock trades up, they exercise the overallotment option and buy the additional shares from the issuer at the offer price. The down-trade cover is the market purchase.

distractorExplanations.b: Buying from the issuer at the offer price is the cover used when the stock trades up and the option is exercised. A down trade is covered by buying in the market.
distractorExplanations.c: A down trade does not cancel the IPO or refund buyers. The syndicate covers the short by purchasing shares in the market.
distractorExplanations.d: Selling more shares would increase the short. Covering the down trade means buying shares in the market.

prompt: A non-U.S. company sells dollar-denominated bonds to investors in the United States. Those bonds are:

options.text: Eurobonds, meaning dollar bonds sold to investors outside the United States
Bulldog bonds, meaning sterling bonds sold in the United Kingdom by a foreign issuer
Yankee bonds, meaning dollar bonds a non-U.S. issuer sells in the United States
Samurai bonds, meaning yen bonds a foreign issuer sells to investors in Japan

explanation: A Yankee bond is a U.S. dollar bond sold in the United States by a non-U.S. issuer. The issuer is foreign, but the sale is made in the U.S. market. A Eurobond, by contrast, is sold outside the home market of the currency.

distractorExplanations.a: Eurobonds are sold outside the country of the currency. Dollar bonds sold in the United States by a foreign issuer are Yankee bonds, not Eurobonds.
distractorExplanations.b: Bulldog bonds are sterling bonds sold in the United Kingdom. A dollar bond sold in the United States by a foreign issuer is a Yankee bond.
distractorExplanations.d: Samurai bonds are yen bonds sold in Japan. Dollar bonds sold in the United States by a non-U.S. issuer are Yankee bonds.

prompt: A leveraged buyout uses high-yield notes and a revolving bank loan. Which prepayment contrast is the usual one?

options.text: Both the notes and the revolver are usually prepayable from issuance, and the notes have no non-call period
The notes often have a non-call period, while the revolver is usually prepayable
The revolver often has a non-call period, while the notes are usually prepayable from issuance
Both the notes and the revolver usually block repayment until late in the life of each instrument

explanation: A high-yield bond often has a non-call period that limits optional redemption for a time. A revolving bank loan is usually prepayable, so the borrower can repay it and borrow again. The point is that contrast, not a particular non-call schedule.

distractorExplanations.a: This treats the notes as freely prepayable. A high-yield bond often has a non-call period, while the revolver is the instrument that is usually prepayable.
distractorExplanations.c: This reverses the two instruments. The revolver is usually prepayable, and the high-yield bond is the one that often has the non-call period.
distractorExplanations.d: A long block on both instruments does not describe the revolver, which is usually prepayable. The bond's protection is a non-call period, not a freeze for most of its life.

prompt: A holding company issues bonds, and the operating company that owns the assets has its own debt. The holding-company bonds are:

options.text: Senior to the operating company's debt because the parent sits above the subsidiary
Equal in claim with the operating company's secured lenders against the operating assets
Secured by the operating plants because the parent owns the equity of that company
Structurally subordinated to debt the operating company has already issued

explanation: Bonds issued at a holding company are structurally subordinated to debt at the operating company. Operating-company creditors are paid from the operating assets first. The holding-company bondholders are left with the residual value, typically the leftover equity in the subsidiary.

distractorExplanations.a: Owning the subsidiary does not put the parent's bonds ahead of operating-company creditors. Those creditors are paid from the operating assets first.
distractorExplanations.b: Holding-company bonds do not rank equally with secured lenders at the operating company. Those lenders are paid from the operating assets first.
distractorExplanations.c: Stock ownership is not a lien on the plants. The holding-company bonds are structurally subordinated, and operating creditors are paid from those assets first.

prompt: A private company plans a Rule 506(b) equity raise. Counsel is asked whether the offering may be posted on the company's public website and whether any buyer may be non-accredited. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The website post is barred; up to 35 non-accredited purchasers must be sophisticated or have a purchaser representative
Posting the deal on the public website is allowed once Form D is filed with the SEC
The company may advertise the deal publicly if buyers self-certify that they are accredited
Rule 506(b) is the resale exemption used to place restricted securities with institutional buyers, which is what Rule 144A does

explanation: Rule 506(b) prohibits general solicitation, so the issuer cannot advertise the offering on a public website. The same exemption still permits sales to accredited investors and to as many as 35 non-accredited purchasers who are sophisticated enough to evaluate the risks, either alone or with a purchaser representative. Form D is a notice filing after the sale, and it does not open the door to public advertising.

distractorExplanations.b: Form D notifies the SEC of a Regulation D sale; filing that notice does not make a public website advertisement lawful under Rule 506(b).
distractorExplanations.c: A self-certification does not authorize general solicitation under Rule 506(b). Public advertising is barred even when buyers say they are accredited.
distractorExplanations.d: Placing restricted securities with institutional buyers is a Rule 144A resale concept. Rule 506(b) is a private-offering exemption that bars public advertising.

prompt: While documenting a Rule 506 offering, counsel finds that a covered person is subject to a disqualifying bad-actor event. What follows for the exemption?

options.text: The event is handled by a risk-factor footnote, and the Rule 506 exemption stays available
That covered person can disqualify the Regulation D exemption for the offering
Bad-actor rules attach to registered initial public offerings and skip private exemptions
Disqualification hits crowdfunding intermediaries and does not reach a Rule 506 exemption

explanation: A disqualifying bad-actor event involving a covered person can knock out the Regulation D exemption for a Rule 506 offering. A risk-factor footnote does not preserve the exemption for that kind of event. The issuer may have a defense if it shows it did not know of the event and could not have known with reasonable care.

distractorExplanations.a: Disclosure can address certain older events, but a disqualifying bad-actor event can remove the Rule 506 exemption rather than leave it in place behind a footnote.
distractorExplanations.c: The bad-actor condition sits on the Regulation D exemption itself. It is not limited to a registered initial public offering.
distractorExplanations.d: Crowdfunding intermediaries have separate bad-actor rules. A covered person's disqualifying event can still disqualify a Rule 506 exemption.

prompt: A growth company wants to sell securities to the public under Regulation A. Which filing path matches that exemption?

options.text: A Form S-1 for a conventional IPO that can be sold once the SEC declares it effective
No SEC filing, because Regulation A is a resale path for institutional buyers
An SEC offering statement; Regulation A exempts the sale from full registration
A public website post under Rule 506(b), which replaces any offering statement

explanation: Regulation A is an exemption from full Securities Act registration, not a conventional IPO. The issuer files an offering statement with the SEC, typically on Form 1-A, and may sell after the SEC qualifies that statement. Qualification of an offering statement is a different process from a registered IPO declared effective on Form S-1.

distractorExplanations.a: Form S-1 is the registration statement for a conventional IPO. Regulation A uses an offering statement and is an exemption from that full registration.
distractorExplanations.b: Regulation A is not a resale exemption for institutional buyers. The issuer files an offering statement with the SEC and waits for qualification.
distractorExplanations.d: Rule 506(b) is a private exemption that bars public advertising. It is not a substitute for the Regulation A offering statement.

prompt: A well-known seasoned issuer wants securities registered so it can take them down on short notice. Which shelf path fits that issuer?

options.text: File a shelf that cannot be used until the Commission declares the registration effective
Rely on Regulation D, because well-known seasoned issuer status is a private-placement category
File a Regulation A offering statement, the format used for seasoned public issuers
File an automatic shelf that becomes effective when the registration is filed

explanation: A well-known seasoned issuer may use an automatic shelf registration statement that becomes effective on filing. Takedowns are not held up for a separate Commission order declaring the shelf effective. That automatic-shelf path is a registered-offering privilege, not a Regulation D placement or a Regulation A offering statement.

distractorExplanations.a: Waiting for the Commission to declare a shelf effective is the path for an issuer that is not using an automatic shelf. A well-known seasoned issuer's automatic shelf is effective when it is filed.
distractorExplanations.b: Well-known seasoned issuer status is a category for registered shelf offerings. It does not turn the financing into a Regulation D private placement.
distractorExplanations.c: Regulation A uses an offering statement for an exempt sale. It is not the automatic shelf available to a well-known seasoned issuer.

prompt: The cover of a follow-on lists one bookrunner and two co-managers. Which firm controls the order book of investor demand?

options.text: The co-managers control the order book and may overrule the bookrunner on allocations
The bookrunner controls the order book and decides how shares are allocated
The independent auditor controls the order book and ranks accounts by fee size
The listing exchange controls the order book and assigns shares after the open

explanation: The bookrunner builds the order book, recommends allocations, and controls that process on a marketed equity offering. Co-managers help market the deal and may see demand, but they do not take the book away from the bookrunner. Auditors and the listing exchange are not running investor orders for the new issue.

distractorExplanations.a: Co-managers help distribute and market the offering. They do not control the order book, and they cannot overrule the bookrunner on allocations.
distractorExplanations.c: The independent auditor reviews the financial statements in the disclosure. The auditor does not collect investor orders or rank accounts for allocation.
distractorExplanations.d: The listing exchange handles trading after the shares are listed. The order book for the offering itself is controlled by the bookrunner.

prompt: The roadshow on a follow-on has ended, and the issuer meets the lead bank that evening. What happens at pricing?

options.text: The offer price is fixed and shares are allocated to investors in the book
The first confidential filing is submitted so the staff can start its review
Roadshow meetings begin and accounts are asked for non-binding indications
Trading opens and the first public trade is adopted as the offer price

explanation: Pricing is the moment the offer price is fixed and shares are allocated against the book of demand. The confidential filing and the roadshow come earlier. The first trade after the open can print above or below the offer price, so that print does not set the price of the allocated shares.

distractorExplanations.b: The first filing starts staff review long before the deal is priced. Pricing is the later step that fixes the offer price and allocations.
distractorExplanations.c: Indications of interest are gathered during the roadshow, before pricing. Pricing is when the price and the allocations are actually set.
distractorExplanations.d: The first public trade is an aftermarket print. It can differ from the offer price, which was already fixed when the shares were allocated.

prompt: An issuer has a shelf with $80 million of securities still unsold and wants to take down $150 million. What must it do?

options.text: Sell the full $150 million on the current shelf, which has no leftover-capacity ceiling
Place the $70 million gap as a Regulation D private sale and keep the shelf untouched
Register more securities; a takedown cannot exceed the amount still registered
Raise the registered amount by revising the prospectus supplement and selling immediately

explanation: A shelf takedown cannot exceed the securities that are still registered. With $80 million left, the issuer cannot sell $150 million off that shelf. The additional amount has to be registered; a used-up balance needs a new registration before more securities can be sold. A prospectus supplement describes a takedown inside the remaining balance and does not increase it.

distractorExplanations.a: The registered balance is a ceiling. An $80 million remainder cannot support a $150 million takedown, so the current shelf is not unlimited.
distractorExplanations.b: A Regulation D sale of the gap would be a separate unregistered offering. It does not enlarge the shelf or turn the whole $150 million into one takedown.
distractorExplanations.d: A prospectus supplement sets the terms of a takedown within the amount already registered. Revising it does not register the extra $70 million.

prompt: A parent will give each shareholder a pro rata number of shares in a subsidiary. Those shares are not sold to the public for cash. What transaction is that?

options.text: A carve-out IPO that sells new subsidiary shares to the public and raises cash
A self-tender in which the parent repurchases its own shares for cash
A rights offering inviting current holders to purchase additional parent shares for cash at a discount
A spin-off that distributes subsidiary shares and does not raise primary cash

explanation: A spin-off distributes shares of a subsidiary to the parent's existing shareholders. The parent is not selling those shares to new public investors for cash, so the distribution does not raise primary proceeds the way a carve-out IPO does. A self-tender and a rights offering both involve cash, which this distribution does not.

distractorExplanations.a: A carve-out IPO sells subsidiary shares to public investors and raises cash. Handing subsidiary shares to existing holders without that sale is a spin-off.
distractorExplanations.b: A self-tender uses cash to buy back the parent's own shares. A spin-off distributes subsidiary shares and does not raise cash from a public sale.
distractorExplanations.c: A rights offering asks holders to pay cash for additional shares. A spin-off delivers subsidiary shares pro rata and does not raise that cash.

prompt: A note indenture lets the issuer redeem early at a price that compensates holders for the yield left on the notes. Which call is that?

options.text: A flat 10-point call premium that stays the same no matter how many coupons remain
A make-whole call that compensates holders for the yield still remaining
A par redemption that returns 100 and pays nothing for the coupons holders give up
A conversion feature that exchanges each note for a fixed number of common shares

explanation: A make-whole call sets the redemption price to compensate holders for the yield they give up over the remaining life of the notes. That price is based on the payments still due, so it is not a flat premium such as 10 points over par. A par call returns 100 without that yield compensation, and a conversion feature swaps the note for equity instead of redeeming it.

distractorExplanations.a: A flat 10-point premium is a fixed call price. A make-whole changes with the yield still owed to holders and is not a single unchanging point premium.
distractorExplanations.c: A par call redeems at 100 and does not compensate holders for the coupons they lose. A make-whole is built to cover that remaining yield.
distractorExplanations.d: Conversion exchanges the note for a set number of common shares. It is not a redemption price that makes holders whole for yield they will not receive.

prompt: A manufacturer funds payroll by selling unsecured notes that mature in a few months. What instrument is it issuing?

options.text: Common stock sold in an equity IPO to fund the company's working capital
A thirty-year mortgage bond secured by a lien on the company's plants
Commercial paper, the short-term unsecured debt the company is selling
Perpetual preferred stock that pays a cumulative dividend and has no maturity

explanation: Commercial paper is short-term unsecured corporate debt, commonly issued with a maturity of nine months or less and used for working capital such as payroll. Selling those notes is a borrowing. It is not an equity IPO, a long-term secured mortgage bond, or preferred stock.

distractorExplanations.a: An equity IPO sells common stock to public investors. These short-term unsecured notes are commercial paper, which is debt.
distractorExplanations.b: A mortgage bond is long-term debt secured by property. Commercial paper matures in months and is unsecured.
distractorExplanations.d: Preferred stock is an equity interest that pays dividends. Commercial paper is a short-term unsecured debt obligation of the company.

prompt: A company wants its existing common shares to start trading on an exchange without a traditional underwritten bookbuild. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: A direct listing can admit existing shares without an underwritten bookbuild
The company is barred from raising primary capital in this listing or any later deal
Underwriters must run a negotiated book and allocate a new issue before listing
Holders must wait for a pro rata rights offering before the shares can trade

explanation: A direct listing can admit existing shares to exchange trading without a traditional underwritten bookbuild that prices and allocates a new issue. Using that path for shares already outstanding does not stop the company from raising primary capital. A primary sale can be included where the listing format allows it, and the company can still sell new shares in a later offering.

distractorExplanations.b: Listing existing shares without an underwritten bookbuild does not bar primary capital. The company can still sell new shares in a qualifying listing or in a later offering.
distractorExplanations.c: A negotiated book that allocates a new issue is the underwritten process this listing skips. Existing shares can begin trading without that bookbuild.
distractorExplanations.d: A rights offering sells shares to existing holders for cash. A direct listing can let already-issued shares trade without a rights offering first.

prompt: A follow-on is launched at 10 million shares. At pricing the book is strong, and the issuer sells 12 million shares in the base deal. What is that change?

options.text: A downsize, because a larger share count shows investors would not support the range
A pulled deal, because the share count is locked once the range has been launched
A rights offering, because the added shares have to be offered pro rata to holders
An upsize, because the strong book supports more shares than were launched

explanation: An upsized deal sells more shares than the number launched in the range because the order book is strong enough to support the larger base deal. Moving from 10 million to 12 million shares at pricing is that increase. It is the opposite of a downsize, and the extra shares are still allocated from the book rather than offered pro rata as rights.

distractorExplanations.a: A downsize cuts the share count when demand is soft. Selling 12 million shares after launching 10 million, on a strong book, is an upsize.
distractorExplanations.b: A strong book is a reason to price a larger base deal, not to pull the offering. The launched share count is not frozen.
distractorExplanations.c: The additional shares in an upsized bookbuilt deal are allocated from the order book. They are not sold pro rata in a rights offering.

prompt: An issuer collects price-and-size bids and sells the shares at the single price that clears the whole offering. What process is that?

options.text: A negotiated bookbuild, with the lead bank choosing the price and the allocations
A Dutch auction, setting one clearing price from the bids that were collected
A reverse inquiry, where one account asks the issuer to print a bond for that account
An at-the-market dribble-out that sells shares over time at prevailing market prices

explanation: A Dutch auction sets a clearing price from investor bids, typically the price at which the full offering can be sold, and successful bidders pay that single price. The lead bank does not negotiate one price and then allocate shares with discretion, which is a bookbuild. The process is also different from a one-off investor inquiry or a gradual at-the-market sale.

distractorExplanations.a: A negotiated bookbuild lets the lead bank set the price and allocate with discretion. A Dutch auction takes one clearing price from the bids themselves.
distractorExplanations.c: Reverse inquiry is an investor asking the issuer for a particular new issue, often a bond. It does not clear an offering at one price drawn from a stack of bids.
distractorExplanations.d: An at-the-market program sells shares gradually into the market over time. A Dutch auction clears a set offering at one price taken from collected bids.

prompt: Arranging banks advance funds so a buyer can close an acquisition before the bond deal is sold. The bonds are expected to repay that advance. What is the advance?

options.text: The permanent bond issue itself, already funded for the life of the acquisition
Mezzanine equity that stays in the capital structure and is not a short-term take-out
A bridge loan: interim financing that the bond offering is meant to take out
A commercial-paper program with no expectation that bonds will refinance the borrowing

explanation: A bridge loan is interim financing that lets the buyer close before the permanent bonds are issued. The bond offering is the expected take-out of that loan. The advance is not itself the long-term bond, a mezzanine equity layer left in place, or a commercial-paper program with no refinancing plan.

distractorExplanations.a: The bonds are the intended permanent financing. The bank advance is temporary funding until those bonds are sold and repay it.
distractorExplanations.b: Mezzanine equity is a subordinated layer meant to stay in the capital structure. A bridge is short-term debt that the bonds are supposed to take out.
distractorExplanations.d: Commercial paper is a separate short-term borrowing program. This advance is a bridge sized to be repaid by the bond offering.

prompt: A dealer is invited to help place shares of an underwritten offering. It is paid for what it sells, and it does not have to buy shares it fails to sell. What is its role?

options.text: An underwriter, the party that commits to buy its allotment even if some shares remain unsold
The bookrunner, because a dealer that calls investors is treated as running the book
A standby purchaser that must buy shares left unsubscribed in a rights offering
A selling-group member, which sells shares but need not buy any unsold remainder

explanation: A selling-group member helps sell the offering and is paid on the shares it places, but it does not promise to purchase the unsold remainder. That purchase commitment belongs to the underwriter. Calling on accounts does not make the dealer the bookrunner, and a standby purchase obligation is a feature of a rights offering.

distractorExplanations.a: The underwriter takes the commitment to buy shares that are not sold. A selling-group member distributes shares without promising to buy the unsold remainder.
distractorExplanations.b: The bookrunner controls the order book. A dealer that only sells shares, with no purchase commitment, is a selling-group member.
distractorExplanations.c: A standby purchaser agrees to buy shares left after a rights offering. This dealer is selling an underwritten deal and has not taken that purchase commitment.

prompt: FINRA Series 79 qualifies individuals to participate in:

Insurance variable annuity sales
Medical licensing

distractorExplanations.a: Real estate brokerage is a different state license; it is not the investment banking activity Series 79 qualifies a person to perform.
distractorExplanations.c: Selling insurance variable annuities is Series 6 or Series 7 work, not the investment banking role covered by Series 79.
distractorExplanations.d: Medical licensing is an unrelated credential and has nothing to do with qualifying for investment banking.
