$5 million (as amended under current SEC rules)
$1,000 total for all issuers combined nationally
Unlimited if the issuer is private with zero disclosure

explanation: Reg CF permits capital formation from retail investors within offering limits and disclosure requirements.

distractorExplanations.a: Mistakes the size of the exemption: $50 billion is far above the $5 million Regulation Crowdfunding cap.
distractorExplanations.c: Mistakes the size of the exemption: a $1,000 nationwide total is not the $5 million Regulation Crowdfunding cap.
distractorExplanations.d: Drops a condition of the exemption: Regulation Crowdfunding requires disclosure and is not an unlimited raise with no disclosure.

prompt: Exchange Act Rule 10b-5 prohibits:

options.text: Short-swing profits by insiders trading within six months
Sales of unregistered securities made without a valid exemption
Fraud in connection with the purchase or sale of securities
Failure to file Form 4 within two business days

explanation: 10b-5 is the principal antifraud rule enforced by SEC and used in insider trading cases. It covers material misstatements and omissions.

distractorExplanations.a: Short-swing profit recovery is Section 16(b), a strict liability rule, not Rule 10b-5 fraud.
distractorExplanations.b: Selling unregistered, non-exempt securities violates Section 5 of the Securities Act, not Rule 10b-5.
distractorExplanations.d: Late Form 4 filings violate Section 16(a) reporting rules, not the Rule 10b-5 antifraud prohibition.

prompt: Regulation FD generally requires that when an issuer discloses material nonpublic information to market professionals or holders, it must:

options.text: Wait until the next quarterly earnings call to disclose the information
File a Form 8-K within four business days in every case
Delay disclosure until the SEC staff has reviewed and approved the release
Make public disclosure of that information simultaneously or promptly

explanation: Reg FD stops selective disclosure of MNPI; public release (e.g., Form 8-K or broad dissemination) must accompany or promptly follow the private communication.

distractorExplanations.a: Waiting for the next earnings call leaves the selective disclosure uncured; Reg FD requires prompt public release.
distractorExplanations.b: Reg FD's prompt standard is generally within 24 hours or before the next market open, not four business days.
distractorExplanations.c: The SEC does not pre-approve issuer releases; the issuer must disclose simultaneously or promptly.

prompt: Regulation M is designed to:

options.text: Prevent issuers and underwriters from manipulating the market price
Limit underwriting compensation to a fair percentage of offering proceeds
Require prospectus delivery to all purchasers in an IPO
Bar insiders from selling shares during the IPO lock-up

explanation: Reg M trading restrictions (Rules 101–105) limit bids, purchases, and shorting around a distribution so the offering is not artificially supported. Other distribution participants are covered too.

distractorExplanations.b: Underwriting compensation limits come from FINRA Rule 5110, not Regulation M.
distractorExplanations.c: Prospectus delivery is a Securities Act Section 5 requirement, not part of Regulation M.
distractorExplanations.d: Lock-ups are contractual agreements with underwriters; Regulation M restricts trading by distribution participants.

prompt: Exchange Act Section 12(g) requires registration when an issuer exceeds thresholds such as:

options.text: More than $10 million in total assets and a class of equity held by 500 or more holders
More than $10 million in assets and a class of equity held by 2,000 or more holders
A class of securities listed on a national securities exchange
Any public offering of debt registered under the Securities Act

explanation: Section 12(g) requires registration when the issuer is over the statutory asset level and a class of equity is held by 2,000 or more holders of record. Five hundred non-accredited holders is the alternative holder count at that same asset level, not a test of 500 holders of every kind.

distractorExplanations.a: Five hundred holders of every kind was the pre-JOBS Act threshold. That 500 figure now applies only to non-accredited holders, and it is an alternative to 2,000 holders of record.
distractorExplanations.c: Exchange listing triggers registration under Section 12(b), not the Section 12(g) asset and holder thresholds.
distractorExplanations.d: A registered debt offering creates Section 15(d) reporting duties, not Section 12(g) equity registration.

prompt: Investment Company Act Section 3(c)(1) allows a private fund to avoid registration if:

options.text: It has no more than 35 non-accredited investors
It sells interests only to qualified purchasers
It has no more than 100 beneficial owners
It has no more than 2,000 holders of record

explanation: 3(c)(1) funds rely on limited investor count and not making a public offering of interests.

distractorExplanations.a: The 35 non-accredited limit belongs to Rule 506(b); Section 3(c)(1) caps beneficial owners at 100.
distractorExplanations.b: Selling only to qualified purchasers is the Section 3(c)(7) exemption, which has no 100-owner cap.
distractorExplanations.d: 2,000 holders is the Exchange Act Section 12(g) registration threshold, not the 3(c)(1) fund limit.

prompt: Rule 701 exempts employee equity compensation offerings if aggregate sales in 12 months do not exceed the greater of:

options.text: $250,000, 5% of total assets, or 5% of outstanding securities
$500,000, 10% of total assets, or 10% of outstanding securities
$1 million, 10% of total assets, or 10% of outstanding securities
$1 million, 15% of total assets, or 15% of outstanding securities

explanation: Rule 701 lets private companies grant equity to employees without full registration within caps and disclosure rules. Outstanding securities are measured by class.

distractorExplanations.a: These caps are far too low; Rule 701 uses $1 million or 15% of total assets or outstanding securities.
distractorExplanations.b: Rule 701 percentage tests are 15%, not 10%, and the dollar floor is $1 million, not $500,000.
distractorExplanations.c: The $1 million floor is right, but Rule 701 uses 15% of assets or outstanding securities, not 10%.

prompt: Section 11 of the Securities Act generally imposes liability for:

options.text: Material misstatements or omissions in a registration statement
Misstatements in a prospectus or oral communication by a seller
Selling securities before the registration statement is effective
Fraudulent statements in a company's periodic 10-K filings

explanation: Section 11 is a core registered-offering liability statute for the registration statement; due-diligence defenses may be available to non-issuer defendants. Liability falls on the issuer and specified offering participants.

distractorExplanations.b: Liability for misstatements in a prospectus or oral communication is Section 12(a)(2); Section 11 covers the registration statement.
distractorExplanations.c: Selling before effectiveness violates Section 5 with rescission under Section 12(a)(1), not Section 11.
distractorExplanations.d: Fraud in periodic Exchange Act filings is pursued under Rule 10b-5 or Section 18, not Securities Act Section 11.

prompt: Exchange Act Section 13(d) requires beneficial ownership reporting on Schedule 13D within:

options.text: Two business days after crossing 5% beneficial ownership
Five business days after crossing 5% beneficial ownership
Ten calendar days after crossing 5% beneficial ownership
45 days after the calendar year-end in which 5% was crossed

explanation: Schedule 13D is the long-form report for a beneficial owner above 5 percent who is not using the passive short form. It discloses the purpose of the acquisition and is due on the SEC's current deadline for that class of equity securities.

distractorExplanations.a: Two business days is the Form 4 deadline for Section 16 insiders, not the Schedule 13D deadline.
distractorExplanations.c: Ten days was the pre-2024 Schedule 13D deadline; SEC amendments shortened it to five business days.
distractorExplanations.d: 45 days after year-end was the old annual Schedule 13G timing for exempt filers, not the 13D deadline.

prompt: Investors bring a Section 11 suit over a material misstatement in the registration statement, naming both the issuer and the lead underwriter. Which statement about the due-diligence defense is correct?

options.text: The issuer has no due-diligence defense; an underwriter can have one
The issuer and the underwriter are both strictly liable, and neither has a due-diligence defense
The issuer may assert a due-diligence defense, while the underwriter is strictly liable
The auditor who expertised the financial statements is the sole defendant with a due-diligence defense

explanation: Section 11 imposes liability for a material misstatement or omission in the registration statement. The issuer is strictly liable and has no due-diligence defense. An underwriter is a non-issuer defendant and can avoid liability by establishing a due-diligence defense.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the issuer's strict liability with the underwriter's position: the issuer has no due-diligence defense, but an underwriter can have one.
distractorExplanations.c: Reverses the defendants: the issuer has no due-diligence defense, and the underwriter is the party that can assert one.
distractorExplanations.d: An expert has a defense as to the expertised portion, but that does not strip the underwriter of a due-diligence defense or give one to the issuer.

prompt: A purchaser alleges a material misstatement in the prospectus and in an oral offer to sell the security. Which liability provision fits that claim?

options.text: Section 12(a)(1), because a prospectus misstatement is charged as a Section 5 violation
Section 12(a)(2), for a material misstatement in a prospectus or oral communication
Section 11, because an oral roadshow statement is treated as part of the registration statement
Section 16(b), because a prospectus misstatement makes the buyer's profit a short-swing profit

explanation: Section 12(a)(2) is the claim for a material misstatement in a prospectus or in an oral communication used to offer the security. Section 12(a)(1) applies when the offer or sale violated Section 5. An oral misstatement sits outside Section 11, which addresses the registration statement.

distractorExplanations.a: Section 12(a)(1) is the rescission claim for a Section 5 violation, such as an unregistered sale, not for a misstatement in the prospectus.
distractorExplanations.c: Section 11 covers a misstatement in the registration statement; a prospectus or oral misstatement is pursued under Section 12(a)(2).
distractorExplanations.d: Section 16(b) forces statutory insiders to disgorge short-swing profits; it does not remedy a misstatement in a prospectus or an oral offer.

prompt: A registered investment adviser crosses 5 percent of a public company's voting shares in the ordinary course of business and has no plan to influence control. Which report fits that holder?

options.text: Schedule 13D, because a stake above 5 percent is reported as an activist position
Form 4, because crossing 5 percent makes the adviser a Section 16 insider
Schedule 13G, the short-form report for a passive institutional holder
Schedule TO, because crossing 5 percent is filed as the start of a tender offer

explanation: A passive institution that holds more than 5 percent in the ordinary course, without a purpose of influencing control, files Schedule 13G. An activist that buys with a plan to influence or change control files Schedule 13D.

distractorExplanations.a: Schedule 13D is the activist report; a passive institution with no control purpose uses Schedule 13G instead.
distractorExplanations.b: Form 4 reports trades by Section 16 officers, directors, and 10 percent holders; this passive stake is a Schedule 13G filing.
distractorExplanations.d: Schedule TO is the tender-offer filing; a passive holding above 5 percent is reported on Schedule 13G, not as a tender.

prompt: On Tuesday a listed company signs a material definitive agreement to acquire a competitor and needs to disclose that event before its next periodic report. Which form reports the current event?

options.text: Form 10-K, which collects material contracts for the annual report
Form 10-Q, which collects current events for the quarterly report
Form S-1, which discloses the agreement by registering the shares to be issued
Form 8-K, the current report for a material event such as this agreement

explanation: Form 8-K is the current report a public company uses to disclose specified material events, including entry into a material definitive agreement. Form 10-K is the annual report and Form 10-Q is the quarterly report.

distractorExplanations.a: Form 10-K is the annual report; a material current event is not saved for that filing and is reported on Form 8-K.
distractorExplanations.b: Form 10-Q is the quarterly report; it does not take the place of the current report for this agreement.
distractorExplanations.c: Form S-1 registers an offering of securities; signing this agreement is a current event reported on Form 8-K.

prompt: The board of a listed company asks shareholders to vote on a negotiated merger. Which filing solicits those votes?

options.text: A Schedule 14A proxy statement sent for the shareholder vote
A Schedule 14D-9 recommendation statement used as the proxy for that merger vote
A Form 8-K current report standing in for the proxy materials on the merger
A Schedule 13D ownership report the company files to solicit the merger votes

explanation: Votes on a merger of a public company are solicited with a proxy statement on Schedule 14A, which describes the transaction and how the board recommends that shareholders vote. Schedule 14D-9 is the target's recommendation in a tender offer, not this proxy.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the merger proxy with a tender-offer form: Schedule 14D-9 is the target's recommendation statement, while merger votes use Schedule 14A.
distractorExplanations.c: A Form 8-K may announce the merger, but it does not solicit shareholder votes; that solicitation is a Schedule 14A proxy statement.
distractorExplanations.d: Schedule 13D is an outsider's beneficial-ownership report; the company solicits merger votes with a Schedule 14A proxy statement.

prompt: An issuer is preparing a registered offering and asks what it may still say in public. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Halt every public statement, including the ordinary product and customer updates the company already releases
Ordinary factual updates may continue; a new campaign to condition the market is gun-jumping
Open a new campaign about the upcoming deal if the ads leave out the word offering
Shift routine business facts into a free writing prospectus and discontinue the regular factual updates

explanation: The company may keep releasing ordinary factual business information of the sort it already publishes in the regular course. A new campaign intended to condition the market for the upcoming offering is gun-jumping and can be an illegal offer under Section 5.

distractorExplanations.a: A full publicity blackout is the mistake; ordinary factual business updates may continue, while a market-conditioning campaign may not.
distractorExplanations.c: Avoiding the word offering does not rescue a new campaign built to warm up buyers; that campaign is gun-jumping.
distractorExplanations.d: A free writing prospectus is a separate writing; ordinary factual updates do not have to stop or move into one.

prompt: The investment-banking team of a broker-dealer is advising on an unannounced acquisition. Why does the firm keep an information barrier between that team and sales and trading?

options.text: So the bankers can brief the desk in time for sales and trading to position ahead of the announcement
So research mentions of the issuer can be pulled from the firm's website until the acquisition closes
So banking staff do not pass material nonpublic information to sales and trading
So a trade by someone on the desk is exempt from insider-trading liability while the deal is quiet

explanation: An information barrier is meant to stop investment-banking staff who possess material nonpublic information from passing it to sales and trading. It is a control against misuse of that information, not permission for the desk to trade ahead of the announcement.

distractorExplanations.a: Briefing the desk so it can trade ahead is the leak the barrier exists to stop, not the reason for having the wall.
distractorExplanations.b: Publication limits on research are a different control; the barrier is there to block material nonpublic information from reaching sales and trading.
distractorExplanations.d: The barrier does not exempt a trade; if material nonpublic information crosses the wall and someone trades on it, liability can still follow.

prompt: A syndicate member in a follow-on distribution wants to bid for the offered shares in the market while the restricted period is running. What does Regulation M Rule 101 provide?

options.text: It restricts that distribution participant from bidding during the restricted period
It directs the participant to keep bidding so the market price of the offered security stays supported
It applies to the issuer alone and leaves syndicate members free to bid through the whole restricted period
It withholds the final prospectus from purchasers until the restricted period has come to an end

explanation: Regulation M Rule 101 restricts distribution participants, including syndicate members, from bidding for or buying the security in distribution during the restricted period. The issuer's own bids are addressed under a separate rule, and Rule 101 is not a prospectus-delivery rule.

distractorExplanations.b: Reverses the restriction: Rule 101 limits bids by a distribution participant during the restricted period instead of requiring those bids.
distractorExplanations.c: Rule 101 applies to distribution participants such as this syndicate member; the issuer is restricted under Rule 102, not left as the only covered party.
distractorExplanations.d: Prospectus delivery is a Section 5 obligation; Rule 101 is a limit on bids and purchases during the restricted period.

prompt: Which line states the long-standing accredited-investor income and net-worth tests?

options.text: Individual income above $150,000, joint income above $250,000, or net worth above $500,000 including the primary residence
Individual income above $100,000, joint income above $300,000, or net worth above $1 million including the primary residence
Individual income above $200,000, joint income above $300,000, or net worth above $1 million excluding the primary residence
A newer professional license or certification standing in place of the individual income, joint income, and net-worth tests for natural persons

explanation: The long-standing accredited-investor tests are individual income above $200,000, or joint income above $300,000 with a spouse or spousal equivalent, in each of the two most recent years with a reasonable expectation of the same income in the current year, or net worth above $1 million excluding the primary residence. A professional certification is a newer, additional path and did not replace these tests.

distractorExplanations.a: Uses the wrong dollar thresholds and counts the home: the income tests are $200,000 and $300,000, and net worth excludes the primary residence.
distractorExplanations.b: Keeps the $300,000 joint-income figure but misses the $200,000 individual test and wrongly counts the primary residence in net worth.
distractorExplanations.d: A professional certification can qualify a person under a newer category; it did not repeal the income and net-worth tests.

prompt: A private company choosing a Rule 506(b) raise is deciding between a private dinner for invited investors, with no public advertising, and a description of the offering on its public website. Which choice can fit Rule 506(b)?

options.text: The public website advertisement, because Rule 506(b) permits general solicitation of investors at large
Neither the dinner nor the website, because Rule 506(b) bars investor contact until Form D is on file
Both the dinner and the website, because a public post is treated the same as a private dinner under Rule 506(b)
The private dinner with no public advertising; the website advertisement cannot

explanation: Rule 506(b) does not allow general solicitation or general advertising. A private dinner with no public advertising can fit that limit. Posting the offering on a public website is general advertising and cannot be used in a Rule 506(b) offering.

distractorExplanations.a: A public website advertisement is general solicitation, which Rule 506(b) forbids; advertising of that kind belongs to Rule 506(c).
distractorExplanations.b: Form D is a notice filed after sales begin; it is not a waiting period that forbids a private dinner with no public advertising.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats the website post as if it were a private dinner; the public advertisement is general solicitation and falls outside Rule 506(b).

prompt: A company lists its common stock on the New York Stock Exchange and then offers that stock to investors in several states. How does state registration usually apply to that offering?

options.text: The states where the shares are offered must still register the offering before sales begin
The state of incorporation registers the offering, and the exchange listing preempts every other state
These covered securities are generally preempted from state registration
State registration is set aside for municipal bonds and still applies in full to this listed common stock

explanation: Securities listed on a national securities exchange are covered securities. Covered securities, including this exchange-listed stock, are generally preempted from state registration, so states generally cannot require the offering to be registered. A notice filing and anti-fraud authority can remain.

distractorExplanations.a: Ignores preemption: exchange-listed covered securities are generally preempted from state registration requirements.
distractorExplanations.b: Preemption of these covered securities is not limited to states other than the state of incorporation; state registration is generally preempted.
distractorExplanations.d: Exchange-listed common stock is itself a category of covered security; preemption is not reserved for municipal bonds.

prompt: SEC enforcement staff send a Wells notice to the head of an investment-banking team. What does that notice tell the recipient?

options.text: The staff intends to recommend enforcement, and the recipient may submit a response
The notice itself is the complaint that starts the case in federal court or before the Commission
The notice is a settled order and already fixes the sanction the staff decided to impose
The investigation has been closed, and the staff will recommend that no action be brought

explanation: A Wells notice tells the recipient that the staff intends to recommend an enforcement action and gives the recipient a chance to submit a Wells response before that recommendation goes forward. The notice is not the complaint that charges the violation.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the notice with the charging document: a Wells notice comes before a complaint and is not itself the complaint.
distractorExplanations.c: A settlement, if one is reached, comes later; the Wells notice only signals an intended recommendation and invites a response.
distractorExplanations.d: The notice does not close the investigation; it says the staff intends to recommend that an enforcement action be brought.

prompt: A broker-dealer has just been admitted to FINRA membership and will conduct an investment-banking business. What must it keep for supervision of that business?

options.text: An unwritten understanding among its principals about how the banking business will be supervised
A copy of the FINRA manual, which stands in for procedures the firm would otherwise have to write
Written supervisory procedures for the securities business it conducts
Written procedures after it opens a second office, with the first office left to oral supervision

explanation: A FINRA member must establish, maintain, and enforce written supervisory procedures reasonably designed to supervise the securities business it conducts and to achieve compliance with applicable securities laws and FINRA rules.

distractorExplanations.a: An unwritten understanding does not meet the supervision rule; the member has to keep written supervisory procedures.
distractorExplanations.b: Keeping the FINRA manual is not a substitute; the firm must maintain its own written supervisory procedures for its business.
distractorExplanations.d: The duty to keep written supervisory procedures applies to the member's business and does not wait until a second office opens.

prompt: A newspaper notice names the issuer, the title of the security, and the managing underwriters, and states that the offering is made by the prospectus. What is that notice?

options.text: The statutory prospectus that buyers must receive as the full disclosure document for the deal
A tombstone, a limited notice of the offering and not the full prospectus
A free writing prospectus that can be delivered in place of the statutory prospectus
A Schedule 14A proxy statement soliciting votes to approve the terms of the offering

explanation: A tombstone is a limited notice of an offering. It may identify the issuer, the security, and the underwriters, and it points readers to the prospectus. It is not the full prospectus and does not replace the statutory prospectus.

distractorExplanations.a: The statutory prospectus is the full offering document; a tombstone is a limited notice and is not that prospectus.
distractorExplanations.c: A free writing prospectus is a different kind of written offer; this notice is a tombstone and is not the full prospectus.
distractorExplanations.d: Schedule 14A solicits proxies; a short notice that points readers to the prospectus is a tombstone, not a proxy statement.

prompt: An issuer closes one exempt offering and, a short time later, starts a second exempt offering to an overlapping group of investors as part of the same financing plan. What can integration do to those offerings?

options.text: Nothing, because each offering keeps the exemption it claimed even when the two closings are part of one plan
It registers the second offering automatically as soon as the first exempt offering has closed
It recasts both offerings as a Rule 144A resale whether or not a qualified institutional buyer participated
It can combine the two so that each offering loses the exemption it claimed

explanation: Offerings that are close in time and part of one financing plan can be integrated. Treated as a single offering, they can fail the conditions of the exemption each one claimed on its own, so each can lose that exemption.

distractorExplanations.a: Separate closings do not guarantee the exemptions survive; offerings that are really one plan can be integrated and lose those exemptions.
distractorExplanations.b: Integration does not register the later deal; the risk is that the exemptions claimed for the two offerings both fail.
distractorExplanations.c: Rule 144A is a resale path for sales to qualified institutional buyers; integration does not turn the two offerings into that kind of resale.

prompt: Meridian Clinics' IPO registration statement highlights adjusted EBITDA, a non-GAAP measure, in the summary of performance. What must the issuer do with that figure?

options.text: Reconcile adjusted EBITDA to the most directly comparable GAAP measure in the filing
Reconcile adjusted EBITDA to the issuer's other non-GAAP figures, such as adjusted revenue
Present adjusted EBITDA with no reconciliation when the GAAP income statement is in the same filing
Present adjusted EBITDA as a GAAP measure once the footnotes list each add-back management used

explanation: Item 10(e) of Regulation S-K requires a non-GAAP measure in a registration statement, such as adjusted EBITDA, to be reconciled to the most directly comparable GAAP measure. The GAAP measure is also given equal or greater prominence, so readers can see what was excluded.

distractorExplanations.b: A bridge from one non-GAAP figure to another does not do the job. The reconciliation has to reach the most directly comparable GAAP measure.
distractorExplanations.c: Including the GAAP income statement elsewhere in the filing does not excuse the non-GAAP highlight. Adjusted EBITDA still has to be reconciled to GAAP.
distractorExplanations.d: Defining the add-backs does not turn EBITDA into a GAAP measure. It stays non-GAAP, and the filing still needs a reconciliation to the comparable GAAP figure.

prompt: Northline's Form S-1 will include the independent auditor's report on the financial statements. What must happen before that report is included?

options.text: The chief financial officer certifies the report as management's own representation of the audit work
The auditor must consent in writing before its audit report goes into the registration statement
The managing underwriter attaches the report after it receives the auditor's signed comfort letter
The listing exchange accepts the report with the listing application and treats that as the auditor's consent

explanation: The auditor is an expert under the Securities Act. Rule 436 requires the auditor's written consent before its audit report is included in the registration statement, and that consent is filed as an exhibit.

distractorExplanations.a: The audit report is the auditor's opinion. The chief financial officer cannot adopt it as management's own representation and skip the auditor's consent.
distractorExplanations.c: A comfort letter is a separate letter to the underwriters. It does not authorize the registration statement to include the audit report.
distractorExplanations.d: Listing approval is not the auditor's consent. The consent has to come from the auditor before the report is included.

prompt: Pellam, an emerging growth company, has not filed its IPO registration statement. Bankers want to test whether investors might have interest. Whom may Pellam contact?

options.text: Retail customers of the syndicate, through a public page that collects indications of interest
The issuer's employees, because a pre-filing conversation with an outside investor is not permitted
Qualified institutional buyers and institutional accredited investors, to gauge their interest
Accredited natural persons, contacted with the same pre-filing materials prepared for institutions

explanation: Securities Act Section 5(d) lets an emerging growth company test the waters with qualified institutional buyers and institutional accredited investors before it files a registration statement. That permission does not cover retail customers or accredited natural persons.

distractorExplanations.a: A public page aimed at retail customers is not a test-the-waters communication. The permitted audience is qualified institutional buyers and institutional accredited investors.
distractorExplanations.b: Pellam is not confined to its own employees. Before filing, it may contact qualified institutional buyers and institutional accredited investors.
distractorExplanations.d: Institutional accredited investors are in the permitted group. Accredited natural persons are not, even if the script was written for institutions.

prompt: An emerging growth company is drafting the audited financial statements for its IPO registration statement. Which statement about those financial statements is correct?

options.text: One audited year is enough, and earlier years may be presented as unaudited management estimates
Audited annual financial statements may be omitted when interim figures are presented in their place
Three audited years are required, and emerging growth company status does not reduce that count
This issuer may present two years of audited financial statements rather than three years

explanation: The JOBS Act lets an emerging growth company present two years of audited financial statements in its IPO registration statement, rather than the three years otherwise required. Scaled disclosure does not drop the audit or shrink the history to a single year.

distractorExplanations.a: Emerging growth company status does not cut the audited history to one year, and it does not let earlier years appear only as management estimates.
distractorExplanations.b: Interim figures do not replace audited annual financial statements. The scaled permission is two audited years, not an unaudited filing.
distractorExplanations.c: Three audited years is the baseline for an IPO issuer that is not an emerging growth company. An emerging growth company may present two.

prompt: After Halden Industrials is public, its chief financial officer sells shares in the open market. Who reports that kind of transaction on Form 4?

options.text: A holder above 5% who is not an officer, a director, or a holder of more than 10%
An officer, a director, or a beneficial owner of more than 10% of the registered class
Every investor who bought in the IPO, whatever that investor's role or percentage owned
The transfer agent, on one form that gathers every open-market sale made during the quarter

explanation: Exchange Act Section 16 requires officers, directors, and beneficial owners of more than 10% of a registered class to report changes in beneficial ownership on Form 4. A holder above 5% who is none of those persons does not use Form 4 for that stake.

distractorExplanations.a: Owning more than 5% without being an officer, director, or more-than-10% holder does not make the person a Section 16 insider. That stake is not reported on Form 4.
distractorExplanations.c: Buying in the IPO does not by itself make an investor a Form 4 filer. Form 4 reports transactions by officers, directors, and more-than-10% holders.
distractorExplanations.d: The transfer agent does not file a combined Form 4 for ordinary shareholder sales. The Section 16 insider reports the insider's own transaction.

prompt: A finance director tells a college friend about an unannounced acquisition so the friend can buy shares first. The friend knows the director may not share that information and that the tip is a personal favor. The friend buys. Why can the friend be liable as a tippee?

options.text: The tipper breached a duty for a personal benefit, and the tippee knew or should have known of that breach
The friend is liable because the friend is an officer or director trading for the friend's own account
The friend is liable for any profitable trade on nonpublic information, even when the tipper breached no duty
Liability requires that the friend paid the director cash for the tip, because a personal favor is not a personal benefit

explanation: Under Dirks, a tippee is liable when the tipper breached a duty by disclosing material nonpublic information for a personal benefit and the tippee knew or should have known of that breach. A tip given as a favor so a friend can trade is that personal benefit. The friend need not be an insider.

distractorExplanations.b: The friend does not have to be an officer or director. Tippee liability follows the tipper's breach for a personal benefit when the friend knew or should have known of it.
distractorExplanations.c: A profitable trade on nonpublic information is not enough. If the tipper breached no duty, the tippee does not inherit one.
distractorExplanations.d: Cash is one form of personal benefit, not the only one. A gift of the information so a friend can trade is a personal benefit, so the favor in this tip supports liability.

prompt: A funding portal is intermediating a Regulation Crowdfunding offering for a private issuer. Which statement about that portal is correct?

options.text: The portal may recommend offerings it believes are suitable for the investors who use the platform
The portal may give investment advice when the advice is spoken and is not posted on the website
The portal must not give investment advice or make recommendations to investors who use it
The portal may rank offerings from strongest buy to weakest if the issuer's offering documents sit beside the rank

explanation: A funding portal may intermediate a Regulation Crowdfunding offering, but the Exchange Act definition of a funding portal bars it from offering investment advice or recommendations. Oral advice and a ranked list of buys are recommendations, not exceptions.

distractorExplanations.a: Telling investors which offerings are suitable is investment advice. A funding portal is not allowed to recommend the securities on its platform.
distractorExplanations.b: The ban is not limited to advice posted on the website. Spoken investment advice and recommendations are also outside what a funding portal may do.
distractorExplanations.d: Ranking offerings as buys is a recommendation. Displaying the issuer's documents next to that rank does not remove the prohibition.

prompt: Keel Marine's registration statement is effective, and the final statutory prospectus is on file. A buyer asks how access-equals-delivery affects receipt of that prospectus. Which statement is right?

options.text: The firm must mail a paper copy of the final prospectus and get proof of delivery before it may send the trade confirmation
Electronic access is for the preliminary prospectus, and the final statutory prospectus still has to be printed and mailed
Effectiveness ends the prospectus requirement, because filing the registration statement by itself completes delivery to the buyer
The buyer may receive the statutory prospectus electronically, and a paper copy is not required in every case

explanation: Access-equals-delivery lets investors receive the final statutory prospectus electronically, including through the filing on EDGAR. A paper copy is not required in every case. The rule changes the method of delivery; it does not cancel the prospectus.

distractorExplanations.a: Access-equals-delivery does not require a mailed paper prospectus, or proof of that mailing, before the confirmation. Electronic access can satisfy delivery of the final prospectus.
distractorExplanations.b: The relief is not limited to the preliminary prospectus. The final statutory prospectus may be made available electronically.
distractorExplanations.c: Filing does not repeal the prospectus. The buyer still receives the statutory prospectus; paper is simply not required in every case.

prompt: A FINRA member is lead underwriter of Arden Foods' initial public offering of common stock. Under the corporate financing rule, what happens to the underwriting terms?

options.text: The member and the issuer may leave the terms off FINRA's docket if both sign the underwriting agreement
The underwriting terms of Arden's public common-stock offering are filed with FINRA for review
FINRA reviews the issuer's business plan and does not take a separate filing of the underwriting terms
The terms stay in the syndicate's files, because the corporate financing rule applies to private placements

explanation: FINRA Rule 5110, the corporate financing rule, requires a member participating in a public offering to file the underwriting terms and arrangements with FINRA. On this initial public offering of common stock, a private agreement does not take the place of that filing.

distractorExplanations.a: Signatures on the underwriting agreement do not keep the terms off FINRA's docket. The corporate financing rule still requires the public offering's underwriting terms to be filed.
distractorExplanations.c: The corporate financing filing covers the underwriting terms and arrangements. It is not a review of the issuer's business plan in place of that filing.
distractorExplanations.d: This filing is for a member's public offering. The terms of Arden's initial public offering are not left solely in the syndicate's files as if the rule covered only private placements.

prompt: North Harbor Securities, a broker-dealer, is writing the procedures it will use when it opens customer accounts. Where does the customer identification program fit?

options.text: It replaces the anti-money-laundering program, so the firm does not need a separate anti-money-laundering policy
It is the sales script the desk uses to decide which new accounts should be offered shares in new issues
The customer identification program is part of this firm's anti-money-laundering compliance
It is required of investment advisers and does not apply when a broker-dealer opens customer accounts

explanation: A broker-dealer's customer identification program is part of its anti-money-laundering compliance. The firm identifies and verifies customers as part of that program. The program does not replace the broader anti-money-laundering duty, and it is not a script for allocating new issues.

distractorExplanations.a: Customer identification does not take the place of the anti-money-laundering program. It is one part of that compliance, and the firm still needs the program.
distractorExplanations.b: The customer identification program is used to know the customer for anti-money-laundering purposes. It is not a sales script for deciding who is offered new issues.
distractorExplanations.d: A broker-dealer that opens customer accounts must keep a customer identification program. The requirement is not limited to investment advisers.

prompt: Investors who bought in a registered offering sue under Section 11 after the shares fall below the price they paid. How does Section 11 measure damages?

options.text: The decline from the amount paid for the shares, with that amount limited by the public offer price
A punitive multiple of the investor's loss, imposed to punish a defective registration statement
The entire price the plaintiff paid, even if the plaintiff already sold the shares for more than that price
The profit the plaintiff expected to earn, with no limit tied to the price at which the securities were offered

explanation: Section 11(e) measures damages by the decline from the amount the plaintiff paid, and that amount paid cannot exceed the public offer price. The statute does not add a punitive multiple of the loss, and it does not award the profit the investor hoped to make.

distractorExplanations.b: Section 11 damages follow the statutory decline from the amount paid. They are not a punitive multiple of the loss aimed at punishing the disclosure.
distractorExplanations.c: The plaintiff does not recover the full price paid without regard to later value. A sale above the amount paid does not produce a Section 11 recovery of that entire price.
distractorExplanations.d: Section 11 does not award the profit the plaintiff expected. Recovery is the decline from the amount paid, and that amount is limited by the offer price.

prompt: Cinder Glass puts next year's revenue projections in its IPO registration statement, with cautionary language beside them. Which statement about the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act safe harbor is correct?

options.text: The cautionary language brings these projections inside the safe harbor for the IPO registration statement
The safe harbor applies if the projections are moved out of the prospectus summary and into the MD&A
The safe harbor applies to these projections because it was written to cover forward-looking statements in initial public offerings
The statutory safe harbor does not apply to forward-looking statements in this IPO registration statement

explanation: The Private Securities Litigation Reform Act safe harbor for forward-looking statements does not apply to statements made in connection with an initial public offering. Cautionary language next to projections in the IPO registration statement does not bring those statements within the statutory safe harbor.

distractorExplanations.a: Cautionary language matters where the safe harbor applies. An IPO registration statement is outside that harbor, so the legend does not place these projections inside it.
distractorExplanations.b: Moving the projections into the MD&A does not change the result. Forward-looking statements in the IPO registration statement stay outside the safe harbor.
distractorExplanations.c: The statute excludes forward-looking statements made in connection with an initial public offering. The safe harbor was not written to cover the IPO registration statement.

prompt: Portage Mills, a listed issuer, is choosing the firm that will audit its financial statements. Who is responsible for appointing that auditor?

options.text: Management, through the chief financial officer who signs the filings and would otherwise select the audit firm
The audit committee, rather than management, is responsible for appointing the outside auditor
The lead underwriter of the issuer's most recent offering, which engaged an auditor during the marketing
The SEC staff member who reviews the issuer's filings and designates an acceptable audit firm

explanation: Under Sarbanes-Oxley and Exchange Act Rule 10A-3, the audit committee of a listed issuer is directly responsible for appointing the external auditor. Management prepares the financial statements, but management is not the body that appoints the auditor.

distractorExplanations.a: The chief financial officer signs filings and management prepares the numbers. Appointing the auditor is the audit committee's responsibility, not management's.
distractorExplanations.c: The lead underwriter's work on an offering does not give it the power to appoint the issuer's auditor. That responsibility belongs to the audit committee.
distractorExplanations.d: The SEC staff reviews disclosure. It does not appoint the issuer's auditor or name the audit firm the issuer must hire.

prompt: An associate at a broker-dealer reports possible securities-law violations to the SEC. The firm then fires the associate because of that report. What does the SEC whistleblower program provide?

options.text: The firm may fire the associate unless the SEC has already paid the associate an award for the report
The firm may fire the associate if the associate also told the firm's compliance department before calling the SEC
The program prohibits retaliation against the whistleblower because of the report to the SEC
The retaliation ban covers employees of public issuers and does not reach an associate fired by a broker-dealer

explanation: Exchange Act Section 21F prohibits an employer from retaliating against a whistleblower because the whistleblower provided information to the SEC. Firing the associate for that report is retaliation. Protection does not wait for an award and is not lost because the associate also spoke to compliance.

distractorExplanations.a: The retaliation prohibition does not wait until the SEC pays an award. It applies when the employer fires a whistleblower for reporting to the SEC.
distractorExplanations.b: Also telling internal compliance does not permit the firing. The program still prohibits retaliation for the report the associate made to the SEC.
distractorExplanations.d: The retaliation ban applies to employers, including a broker-dealer. It is not limited to employees of public issuers.

prompt: Before a syndicate uses a proposed structure, counsel describes it to the SEC staff and receives a no-action letter. What is that letter?

options.text: A statute that later transactions of the same type are required to follow
A court ruling that decides the request and controls later disputes on similar facts
A Commission regulation adopted through notice-and-comment rulemaking, with the force of a rule
It is staff guidance, not a statute enacted by Congress and not a court ruling

explanation: A no-action letter is informal staff guidance. The staff states that it will not recommend enforcement action if the facts match the request. The letter is not a statute enacted by Congress, and it is not a ruling issued by a court.

distractorExplanations.a: Congress did not enact the letter. A no-action letter is the staff's guidance on the facts in the request, not a statute later deals must follow.
distractorExplanations.b: No court heard the request. A no-action letter is staff guidance, not a judicial ruling and not a precedent decided in a case.
distractorExplanations.c: The staff did not adopt the letter as a Commission regulation through notice and comment. It remains staff guidance, not a legislative rule.
